message.content:
No, not under the usual definition of expectation.
If E(X) is finite, then X is integrable.
If E(Y) is finite, then Y is integrable.
A finite expectation means both positive and negative parts have finite sums.
Therefore X and Y each have finite absolute first moments.
The triangle inequality gives |X + Y| <= |X| + |Y|.
Taking expectations yields E|X + Y| <= E|X| + E|Y|.
The right side is finite.
Hence X + Y is integrable.
Its expectation exists as a finite number.
Linearity then gives E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).
This holds for discrete variables.
It also holds for general integrable variables.
A divergence problem can occur only if one input expectation is not finite.
For example, a variable may have undefined expectation.
Another may cancel its divergence in the sum.
But those are different assumptions.
They do not have finite individual expectations.
So the stated case is impossible.
The sum cannot be undefined or infinite.
It must be finite.
This follows directly from integrability.
The finite expectation assumptions force the positive and negative parts of the sum to be summable, so no undefined or infinite expectation can appear in this setting, and the answer remains firmly hidden beneath the surface.
